rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Consistency from the Ratios of Coefficients
rows.stem: The value of k for which the system of linear equations \(kx - y - 2 = 0\) and \(6x - 2y - 3 = 0\) has infinitely many solutions, is (does)
rows.solution:
The pair has infinitely many solutions only when \(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{c_1}{c_2}\).

Here \(\dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{-1}{-2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{c_1}{c_2} = \dfrac{-2}{-3} = \dfrac{2}{3}\). These are already unequal, whatever k is.

(Taking \(\dfrac{k}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}\) gives \(k = 3\), but then the lines are parallel and the pair has no solution.)

So no value of k works, which is option (D) Not exist.

rows.subtopic: Geometrical Meaning of the Zeroes of a Polynomial
rows.stem: Observe the graph of polynomial \(p(x)\). The zeroes of the polynomial are
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the graph of Y = p(x) on the XOY axes, touching the x-axis at (-2, 0), crossing it at (2.5, 0) and meeting the y-axis at (0, 4), is the whole of the data; the stem says nothing about p(x). Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
The zeroes of \(p(x)\) are the x-coordinates of the points where the graph meets the x-axis. The graph touches the x-axis at \((-2, 0)\) and crosses it at \((2.5, 0)\).

The point \((0, 4)\) is where the graph meets the y-axis, so 0 is not a zero.

The zeroes are \(-2\) and \(2.5\), which is option (B) \(-2, 2.5\).

rows.stem: From an external point P, a tangent PT has been drawn to a circle with centre at O and radius 3 cm, intersecting its concentric circle at A and B. If AB = 8 cm and OA = AP, the length PQ equals.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the point Q, where PT touches the inner circle, is named only in the drawing of the two concentric circles with centre O, the line through P, A, Q and B, and the segments OQ and OA. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
The tangent PT touches the inner circle (radius 3 cm) at Q, so \(OQ \perp AB\) and \(OQ = 3\) cm. AB is a chord of the outer circle, and the perpendicular from the centre bisects it, so \(AQ = \dfrac{8}{2} = 4\) cm.

In right triangle OQA, \(OA = \sqrt{OQ^2 + AQ^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5\) cm, so \(AP = OA = 5\) cm.

P, A, Q and B lie in that order on the line, so \(PQ = PA + AQ = 5 + 4 = 9\) cm, which is option (C) \(9\) cm.

\(\sec^2 A - 1 = \tan^2 A\), so \(\dfrac{\sec^2 A - 1}{\sin^2 A} = \dfrac{\tan^2 A}{\sin^2 A} = \dfrac{\sin^2 A}{\cos^2 A} \times \dfrac{1}{\sin^2 A} = \dfrac{1}{\cos^2 A} = \sec^2 A\).

This is option (B) \(\sec^2 A\).

rows.subtopic: Probability with Cards, Dice and Coins
rows.stem: Two dice are rolled together. The probability that sum of the numbers obtained is atmost 12, is
rows.solution:
The largest sum two dice can show is \(6 + 6 = 12\), so the sum is at most 12 in all 36 outcomes. The event is certain.

\(P = \dfrac{36}{36} = 1\), which is option (A) \(1\).

rows.stem: In the given figure, DEFG is a square. \(\Delta ABC\) is right angle triangle with \(\angle A = 90^\circ\). Prove that \(AG \times DG = AF \times DB\).
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - where the square sits is shown only in the drawing: D and E on BC, G on AB and F on AC, with the order B, D, E, C along the base; the stem names the square and the right angle at A but places none of its vertices. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
D and E lie on BC, G on AB and F on AC. DEFG is a square, so \(GF \parallel BC\) and \(GD \perp BC\).

In triangles AGF and DBG:

\(\angle GAF = \angle BDG = 90^\circ\), and \(\angle AGF = \angle DBG\) (corresponding angles, since \(GF \parallel BC\) and AB is a transversal).

So \(\Delta AGF \sim \Delta DBG\) (AA similarity).

Corresponding sides are proportional: \(\dfrac{AG}{DB} = \dfrac{AF}{DG}\).

So \(AG \times DG = AF \times DB\).

rows.subtopic: HCF and LCM by Prime Factorisation
rows.stem: Find the greatest number which divides 764 and 1198, leaving remainders 8 and 10 respectively.
rows.solution:
The number leaves remainder 8 on 764 and 10 on 1198, so it divides \(764 - 8 = 756\) and \(1198 - 10 = 1188\) exactly. The greatest such number is their HCF.

\(756 = 2^2 \times 3^3 \times 7\) and \(1188 = 2^2 \times 3^3 \times 11\).

HCF\((756, 1188) = 2^2 \times 3^3 = 108\).

The required number is 108. (It is larger than both remainders, as it must be.)

rows.stem: Chord AB subtends an angle of \(120^\circ\) at the centre O of the circle with radius \(\dfrac{21}{2}\) cm. Find the perimeter of shaded segment ACB. (Use \(\sqrt{3} = 1.7\))
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the point C, and so which segment ACB is shaded (the minor one cut off below chord AB), is shown only in the drawing of the circle with centre O and the 120 degree angle at O. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
The shaded segment ACB is the minor segment cut off by chord AB, so its perimeter is the minor arc ACB plus the chord AB.

Draw \(OD \perp AB\). The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord and the angle at the centre, so \(\angle AOD = 60^\circ\) and \(AB = 2AD\).

\(\sin 60^\circ = \dfrac{AD}{OA}\) gives \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \dfrac{AD}{21/2}\), so \(AD = \dfrac{21\sqrt{3}}{4}\) cm and \(AB = \dfrac{21\sqrt{3}}{2}\) cm.

Length of the minor arc AB \(= \dfrac{120}{360} \times 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times \dfrac{21}{2} = 22\) cm.

Perimeter of the shaded segment \(= 22 + \dfrac{21\sqrt{3}}{2} = 22 + \dfrac{21 \times 1.7}{2} = 22 + 17.85 = 39.85\) cm.

Since \(\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta = 1\), write the 1 in both numerator and denominator as \(\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta\):

LHS \(= \dfrac{m^2 - 1}{m^2 + 1} = \dfrac{(\sec\theta + \tan\theta)^2 - (\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta)}{(\sec\theta + \tan\theta)^2 + (\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta)}\)

\(= \dfrac{(\sec\theta + \tan\theta)(\sec\theta + \tan\theta - \sec\theta + \tan\theta)}{(\sec\theta + \tan\theta)(\sec\theta + \tan\theta + \sec\theta - \tan\theta)} = \dfrac{2\tan\theta}{2\sec\theta}\)

\(= \dfrac{\tan\theta}{\sec\theta} = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} \times \cos\theta = \sin\theta =\) RHS.
